# CHAPTER 10: Trees Plus

© Repina Valeriya/Shutterstock

In [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08), we explored the implementation of the Binary Search Tree ADT and how its search operations (`FindNode`) could potentially achieve the same O(log[2]N) search efficiency as applying binary search to a sorted list. The caveat is that the binary search tree must be balanced to achieve this performance behavior.

We assumed that the items in the binary search tree were inserted in random order. In practice, this typically leads to short and “bushy” trees that minimize the distance from the root node, thus facilitating fewer comparisons and maximizing the efficiency. However, we could easily achieve the worst case by inserting elements in sorted order, which leads to a degenerate tree that is nothing more than a linked list, with O(N) search performance. In general, the adding and removing of nodes from a binary search tree does not ensure that the tree maintains balance and can lead to trees that are no longer efficient.

In this chapter, we explore extensions to our Binary Search Tree ADT so that it self-balances as nodes are inserted. That is, operations that modify the binary search tree will perform some additional work to maintain balance, thus retaining the desired performance characteristics.

### 10.1 AVL Trees

Recall that a binary search tree T is balanced if the difference between the number of nodes in the left subtree of T and in the right subtree of T is not more than 1\. This difference is often referred to as a tree’s [balance factor](#bm01.xhtml_gloss012). Depending on how elements are inserted into a binary search tree, some trees will be balanced and others will not. The nodes in a binary search tree can be rearranged to produce a balanced binary search, as we saw in our implementation of heaps in [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09). Unfortunately, for trees that change frequently, it is not clear how often rebalancing should occur. If we rebalance the tree too often, it can lead to wasted work for trees that are mostly balanced to begin with.

You might then wonder if there is a way to easily detect if a tree becomes unbalanced when an element is inserted or removed. If so, then perhaps an efficient rebalancing operation exists that we can use in the context of an insertion or removal. The notion of rebalancing a tree in the context of insertion and removal operations was first proposed in 1962 by two Soviet mathematicians, Georgii Adelson-Velskii and Evgenii Landis, with a self-balancing binary search tree named after its inventors, called an [AVL tree](#bm01.xhtml_gloss011).

An AVL tree operates in O(log[2]N) time in both the average and worst cases for lookup, insertion, and removal of nodes. To maintain this efficiency, an AVL tree must rebalance itself after any operation that could potentially lead to an unbalanced shape.

Because the insertion and removal operations can disrupt the balance of a binary search tree by adding and removing nodes, these operations are extended by an AVL tree implementation to rebalance when any changes are made to the tree. In particular, after the usual insertion or removal is performed, it is followed with the application of one or more operations called tree rotations to regain balance if the heights of the two subtrees of any node differ by more than 1\. In such a case, the tree is no longer an AVL tree.

There are four rotation cases that we must consider to fix an AVL tree if the tree is not balanced. The first two cases involve “rotating” a node in either the left or right direction. This rotation operation simply means that we make a child node the parent of its current parent. The direction in which we rotate depends on the structure of the tree. In certain circumstances, a single left or right rotation is not enough to correct the imbalance. Fortunately, there are only two additional cases to consider that require two rotation operations. The structure of the tree and the location of the node inserted (or deleted) will tell us if we need to perform a left rotation followed by a right, or a right rotation followed by a left. We summarize each case next to guide you through our detailed discussion of when and how they should be applied.

An imbalance in an unbalanced node T of an AVL tree can be resolved as follows:

1.  If the node was inserted into the the left subtree of node T’s left child S, then we apply right rotation.

2.  If the node was inserted into the right subtree of T’s right child S, then we apply left rotation.

3.  If the node was inserted into the left subtree of T’s right child, then we apply right-left rotation.

4.  If the node was inserted into the right subtree of T’s left child, then we apply left-right rotation.

#### Single Rotations on AVL Trees

[Figure 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig1) shows two binary search trees. The tree on the left is an AVL tree because the heights of the two subtrees of all nodes differ by at most 1, whereas the tree on the right is not an AVL tree because the heights of the left and right subtrees of the node with value 6 differ by 2\. In our discussion on AVL trees, we will focus on inserting elements into an AVL tree and leave node removal as an exercise.

A node whose balance factor is at most 1 is often referred to as a [balanced node](#bm01.xhtml_gloss013), whereas a node whose balance factor is greater than 1 can be referred to as an [unbalanced node](#bm01.xhtml_gloss149). Thus, in [Figure 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig1), the node with value 6 in the tree on the left is a balanced node because its balance factor is at most 1, and the node with value 6 in the tree on the right is an unbalanced node because its balance factor is greater than 1.

In [Figure 10.2](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig2), we see the insertion of the values 6, 4, and 2 into an empty AVL tree. After inserting 6 and 4, the tree remains balanced, so no adjusments need to be made. However, after we insert 2, the tree becomes unbalanced with respect to the node whose value is 6\. That is, the height of its left subtree is 2 and the height of its right subtree is 0\. Because the difference is greater than 1, it breaks the rule that the subtrees of all nodes must differ at most by 1\. To fix the unbalanced tree, it must be reorganized by applying a [right rotation](#bm01.xhtml_gloss120) operation to the root node of the left subtree that causes the imbalance. The right rotation is so called because it appears as though we are rotating nodes around the root of the left subtree (4). What we are really doing is making the parent of the left subtree’s root node (6) the right child of the left subtree’s root node (4).

![](Images/f10-01.jpg)

Figure 10.1 An AVL tree and a tree that is not an AVL tree

![](Images/f10-02.jpg)

Figure 10.2 Right rotation on an unbalanced tree

![](Images/f10-03.jpg)

Figure 10.3 Left rotation on an unbalanced tree

Likewise, it is possible to insert elements into a tree such that we must perform a rotation in the right subtree. As shown in [Figure 10.3](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig3), if we insert the values 2, 4, and 6 into a fresh AVL tree, we have an unbalanced node (2) because its right subtree is contributing to a balance factor greater than 1\. To remedy the problem, we perform a [left rotation](#bm01.xhtml_gloss086) operation. In this case, we are rotating around 4.

#### Generalizing Single Rotations on AVL Trees

More generally, if the balance factor of a node is greater than 1, then we either rotate right, if the height of the left subtree is larger than the right, or we rotate left, if the height of the right subtree is larger.

Thus far, we’ve looked at rotations of single nodes. Of course, we can also end up inserting into the middle of an existing tree. In [Figure 10.4](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig4), we see that the unbalanced node T has a left subtree (A) rooted at node S whose height is greater than T’s right subtree (C). We perform a right rotation around T to restore balance. This is accomplished by making T the right subtree of S and the original right subtree of S (B) becomes T’s left subtree. Because an insertion of a node can only increase the height of a subtree by 1, and a right (or left) rotation can only decrease the height of a subtree by 1, an unbalanced subtree becomes balanced following the application of a tree rotation.

Similarly, in [Figure 10.5](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig5), we show the general operation of a left rotation. We see that the unbalanced node T has a right subtree (C) rooted at S whose height is larger than T’s left subtree (A). We perform a left rotation around T to restore balance. This is accomplished by making T the left subtree of S, and then the original left subtree of S (B) becomes T’s right subtree. Following the left-rotate operation, the tree is once again balanced.

Determining which rotation to apply depends on which subtree of T received an additional node and whether that addition created an imbalance. If there is an imbalance and the node was inserted into the left subtree of T’s left child S, then a right rotation is applied. If the node was inserted into the right subtree of T’s right child S, then a left rotation is applied.

![](Images/f10-04.jpg)

Figure 10.4 Right rotation on an AVL tree to maintain balance

![](Images/f10-05.jpg)

Figure 10.5 Left rotation on an AVL tree to maintain balance

In [Figure 10.6](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig6), we show the application of right rotation to an existing AVL tree after inserting an element. In (a), we have a balanced AVL tree before any node insertion. We then insert the element 1 into our AVL tree (b), which creates a new node that is the left child of the node with value 2\. Node T becomes unbalanced, as its balance factor is 2, and we must perform right rotation around 11, as depicted in [Figure 10.6c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig6). We make T a right subtree of S ([Figure 10.6d](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig6)), followed by making S’s right subtree a left subtree of T ([Figure 10.6e](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig6)). Performing left rotation operates similarly.

The following algorithm performs the right rotation on a given unbalanced node. You can assume a sensible definition for a binary tree node with both a left and right child, as described in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08).

As you can see, this algorithm is straightforward and mirrors the steps in [Figure 10.6](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig6). We can design an algorithm to rotate left in a similar fashion.

![](Images/f10-06.jpg)

Figure 10.6 Right rotation on AVL tree after insert

You might begin to wonder if a single right or left rotation is the only necessary operation to restore balance to an AVL tree. To answer this question, we can look at another AVL tree example, which we will do next.

#### Double Rotations on AVL Trees

In [Figure 10.7a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7), we have a balanced AVL tree; however, after we insert 60 in [Figure 10.7b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7), the AVL tree becomes unbalanced. To rebalance the tree requires a right rotation around the node containing 72 ([Figure 10.7c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7)). Unfortunately, the resulting tree ([Figure 10.7d](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7)) still remains unbalanced. To fix this, we perform an additional left rotation around the node containing 50, as shown in [Figure 10.7e](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7). The final balanced tree can be seen in [Figure 10.7f](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig7). When an addition to an AVL tree occurs in the left subtree of T’s right child, we apply a double rotation called a [right-left rotation](#bm01.xhtml_gloss119).

![](Images/f10-07.jpg)

Figure 10.7 Right-left rotation on AVL tree after insert

Similarly, in [Figure 10.8a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8), we have a balanced AVL tree that becomes unbalanced with the insertion of 13 ([Figure 10.8b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8)). This requires a left rotation around the node containing 12 ([Figure 10.8c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8)), resulting in the tree shown in [Figure 10.8d](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8). Unfortunately, the tree is still unbalanced, requiring an additional right rotation around 17 ([Figure 10.8e](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8)) to restore the balance. The resulting balanced tree is depicted in [Figure 10.8f](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig8). When an addition to an AVL tree occurs in the right subtree of T’s left child, we apply a double rotation called a [left-right rotation](#bm01.xhtml_gloss085).

Unlike the previous examples, in both of these cases, the rotation operations were not applied to a direct child of the unbalanced node. Rather, they were invoked upon the great-grandchild. In addition, they required two rotation operations to restore balance to the AVL tree.

![](Images/f10-08.jpg)

Figure 10.8 Left-right rotation on AVL tree after insert

#### Generalizing Double Rotations on AVL Trees

In [Figure 10.9](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig9), we see the general structure for performing right-left rotation after an element is inserted into an AVL tree. [Figure 10.9a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig9) shows a node insertion into the left subtree of S (G) of the node T. This insertion causes T to become unbalanced; however, the imbalance manifests itself under a great-grandchild of T (G) rather than under S itself. For this reason, we require a right rotation around G in an attempt to restore balance ([Figure 10.9b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig9)). As you can see, this does not lead to a balanced AVL tree. To complete the balance, we must perform an additional left rotation around G to regain balance, as shown in [Figure 10.9c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig9).

Likewise, the general case for left-right rotation is depicted in [Figure 10.10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig10), where a new node is created under the right subtree G of T’s left child S. Once again, T becomes the first unbalanced node along the path to the insertion point. As [Figure 10.10a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig10) shows, we must perform a left rotation around T’s great-grandchild node G to restore balance. This moves us in the necessary direction; however, a right rotation around G ([Figure 10.10b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig10)) is also needed to regain a balanced AVL tree ([Figure 10.10c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig10)).

![](Images/f10-09.jpg)

Figure 10.9 General right-left rotation on AVL tree

![](Images/f10-10.jpg)

Figure 10.10 General left-right rotation on AVL tree

The algorithm for right-left and left-right rotation mirrors the illustrations for double-rotation given previously. Note that we can use our previous algorithm definitions for rotate right and rotate left to implement these algorithms.

To summarize, the imbalance of an AVL tree can occur after inserting an element into a balanced AVL tree. Because the tree was balanced before the insertion, there will be at most a single unbalanced node T along the path to the newly inserted node. Restoring balance requires either a right, left, right-left, or left-right rotation. No other operations are needed to restore balance. We can summarize these rules as follows.

An imbalance in an unbalanced node T of an AVL tree can be resolved as follows

1.  If the node was inserted into the left subtree of node T’s left child S, then we apply right rotation.

2.  If the node was inserted into the right subtree of T’s right child S, then we apply left rotation.

3.  If the node was inserted into the left subtree of T’s right child, then we apply right-left rotation.

4.  If the node was inserted into the right subtree of T’s left child, then we apply left-right rotation.

To help solidify your understanding of these operations, we show a taxonomy ([Table 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_ch10table1)) of the possible insertion points with respect to trees T and S, as shown in [Figures 10.9](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig9) and [10.10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig10), respectively. This makes it clear which operations should be applied, based on where the insertion occurred.

Deleting nodes from an AVL tree may also introduce imbalance. The procedure for detecting the imbalance and reshaping the tree to restore balance is the same as the procedure for insertion. That is, if removing a node causes an imbalance in an AVL tree, we identify the unbalanced node T that is nearest to the deleted node and perform one of the afore mentioned operations, depending on where the node was deleted with respect to T. We leave the removal operation as an exercise.

|  |  |  | Insertion occurred in right-left subtree of S |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Left child of S | Right child of S |
| Insertion occurred in right-left child of subtree T | Left child of T | Right rotation | Left-right rotation |
| Right child of T | Right-left rotation | Left rotation |

Table 10.1 AVL Rotation Taxonomy

#### Application Level

From the user’s perspective, an AVL tree is operationally no different than the Binary Search Tree ADT. However, depending on the problem that we are trying to solve and the data that we are representing, the choice of using an AVL tree over the standard binary search tree will make a difference in the application domain. For example, with problems involving data that are sufficiently random and remain unchanged after the tree is created, a binary search tree is a good choice. In this case, we insert all the data into the tree and perform a final balancing operation on the tree to achieve efficient search performance. A good example of this is a dictionary application, where words are rarely added or removed.

Problems involving data that change frequently over time would dictate the use of a self-balancing binary search tree such as the AVL tree. In this case, the slight overhead of balancing during insertion and removal of nodes is outweighed by the advantage of guaranteed efficient O(log[2]N) search performance. Consider a Twitter application where hashtags are used to index tweets. Twitter hashtags are constantly changing; new ones are introduced, old ones become obsolete, and the searching of hashtags is a frequent action performed by users. An AVL tree would be a better choice for this application to ensure efficient searching.

#### Logical Level

The definition of an AVL tree ADT from the logical level requires only minor changes from that of the binary tree that we discussed in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08). In particular, an AVL tree behaves the same way in all operations except those that modify the tree. For this reason, we provide updated specifications for the `PutItem` and `DeleteItem` methods of the TreeADT that highlight the property of balance before and after the invocation of these methods. See [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08) to review the details of the tree structure and other associated methods.

#### Implementation Level

We have already discussed four algorithms that are used to maintain balance in an AVL tree in the context of node insertion and deletion. Each algorithm assumed that the node passed to it is a previously determined unbalanced node. To complete the picture, we will implement each of these algorithms as separate utility methods in our `AVLTreeADT` class. In addition, we need to implement a `Difference` method that identifies an unbalanced node and a `Balance` method for determining which rotation method to apply in the event of imbalance, and then update the `PutItem` method to invoke `Balance` when imbalance occurs. We leave the `DeleteItem` method as an exercise.

Fortunately, the algorithms for each of the rotation operations can easily be translated into C++. To help see the similarity, we repeat the definition of these algorithms here.

The corresponding C++ code for rotate right is as follows:

```
TreeNode* RotateRight(TreeNode* T)

// Returns the tree node resulting from a right rotation.

{

  TreeNode* S = T->left;

  TreeNode* B = S->right;

  S->right = T;

  T->left = B

  return S;

}
```

As you can see, the implementation given here corresponds directly to the algorithm that we defined, except that we are using TreeNode and its left and right fields, as defined in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08). We retained the variables used in our algorithm definitions to make the connection more explicit. The algorithm for rotate left is as follows:

The corresponding C++ code for rotate left is as follows:

```
TreeNode* RotateLeft(TreeNode* T)

// Returns the tree node resulting from a left rotation.

{

  TreeNode* S = T->right;

  TreeNode* B = S->left;

  S->left = T;

  T->right = B

  return S;

}
```

Again, we made the variable names consistent with the algorithm definitions for clarity. Note that we could eliminate the intermediate variable B to shorten the code.

We can then call these methods from our double rotation methods. If you recall, our pseudocode algorithms for right-left and left-right rotation leveraged the existence of right and left rotation. Here is the algorithm again:

The corresponding C++ code is a straightforward implementation:

```
TreeNode* RotateRightLeft(TreeNode* T)

// Returns the tree node resulting from a right-left rotation.

{

  TreeNode* S = T->right;

  T->right = RotateRight(S);

return RotateLeft(T);

}
```

Likewise, the C++ for the `RotateLeftRight` mirrors the algorithm definition:

```
TreeNode* RotateLeftRight(TreeNode* T)

// Returns the tree node resulting from a left-right rotation.

{

  TreeNode* S = T->left;

  T->left = RotateLeft(S);

  return RotateRight(T);

}
```

With our rotation methods in place, we have only the `Difference` method to implement before we are ready to tackle balancing. To determine if a given node T in an AVL tree is unbalanced, we need to check whether the difference between the heights of T’s left and right subtrees is greater than 1\. Thus, to determine the difference, we must find the height of each subtree of T and subtract. In our implementation we subtract the hight of the right subtree from the left. You can subtract the left from the right; however, our implementation of the Balance function described next assumes this implementation and would need to be adjusted accordingly. Here is the code that implements the `Difference` method:

```
int Difference(TreeNode* T) const

// Returns the difference between the heights of the left and right subtrees of T.

// Assumes the given TreeNode* T is not null.

{

   return Height(T->left) – Height(T->right);

}

int Height(TreeNode* T) const

// Returns the height of a tree T.

{

  if (T == null)

    return 0;

  else {

    int heightLeft = Height(T->left);

    int heightRight = Height(T->right);

    if (heightLeft > heightRight)

      return heightLeft + 1;

    else

      return heightRight + 1;

 }

}
```

`Difference` receives a pointer to the `TreeNode` `T` and returns the difference between `T`’s left and right subtree. To determine the difference, we must compute the height of each subtree of `T`. `Height` is a recursive utility method that will return 0 if the pointer to the given `TreeNode` is null (base case); otherwise, it will compute the height of its subtree recursively and add 1, depending on the greater height of the left or the right subtree.

It is important to note that the value returned from `Difference` will be either positive or negative. We can use this information to determine which subtree received the node addition (or deletion). That is, if the `Difference` method returns a positive value, it indicates that the change occurred in the left subtree. If `Difference` returns a negative value, the change occurred in the right subtree. Because we are returning a positive or negative value, we must consider each case in our implementation of `Balance.`

Now that we have all the necessary utility methods, we are ready to implement the `Balance` method. The `Balance` method will be called after each recursive call to the `Insert` method (see [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08) for the definition of `Insert`). In other words, upon returning from each recursive call to `Insert`, we invoke `Balance` to determine if our insertion caused an imbalance and to perform the proper rotation operation, depending on which subtree the new node was inserted into. This is captured more formally in the following pseudocode algorithm:

We first determine if the difference in T’s subtrees is greater than or less than 1\. In either case, it indicates that node T is an unbalanced node, whose subtree incurred the modification, and that rotation must be applied. To determine which rotation operation to invoke, we check T’s left and right subtrees to identify if single rotation or double rotation is necessary. Here is the C++ code that implements this algorithm:

```
TreeNode* Balance(TreeNode* T)

// Checks and balances the subtree T.

{

  int balanceFactor = Difference(T);

  if (balanceFactor > 1) {

    if (Difference(T->left) > 1)

      return RotateRight(T);

    else

      return RotateLeftRight(T);

  }

  else if (balanceFactor < -1) {

    if (Difference(T->right) < 0)

      return RotateLeft(T);

    else

      return RotateRightLeft(T);

  }

  else

    return T;

}
```

Although the code for the `Balance` method appears complicated, it follows directly from our discussion of AVL trees and the pseudocode algorithms that we have developed. Each rule application is carefully determined by the value and sign of the current node’s balance factor.

To close our discussion of the AVL tree, we illustrate the use of the `Balance` method in the context of inserting nodes into an AVL tree. As we mentioned previously, we can rely upon the existing code for inserting nodes into binary trees. That is, in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08), we developed the utility method `Insert`, which is the workhorse method called by `PutItem` to insert a new element into a binary tree. Transforming a standard binary tree into an AVL tree simply requires that we plug in calls to `Balance` at precisely the right moment. The following code reimplements `Insert` with calls to `Balance` highlighted:

```
void Insert(TreeNode*& tree, ItemType item)

// Inserts item into tree.

// Post: item is in tree; search property is maintained.

{

  if (tree == NULL)

  {// Insertion place found.

    tree = new TreeNode;

    tree->right = NULL;

    tree->left = NULL;

    tree->info = item;

  }

  else if (item < tree->info) {

    Insert(tree->left, item);      // Insert in left subtree.

    tree->left = Balance(tree->left);

  }

  else {

    Insert(tree->right, item);     // Insert in right subtree.

    Tree->right = Balance(tree->right);

  }

}
```

Recall that `Insert` is a recursive method that travels down the binary tree looking for the best place to insert the new item. When there are no more child nodes to traverse, the insertion point has been found. We create a new node and begin to unwind our recursive calls. The two calls to `Balance` transform the standard binary tree into an AVL tree. As previously described, we need to invoke `Balance` upon the subtree that has incurred the insertion. Although balancing the AVL tree requires additional work to maintain balance, the extra cost in time is amortized by the reduced cost in search time.

To complete the implementation for inserting new items into an AVL tree, we must update the `PutItem` method with a call to `Balance` on the root node (see highlighted lines):

```
void TreeType::PutItem(ItemType item)

// Calls the recursive function Insert to insert item into tree.

{

  Insert(root, item);

  root = Balance(root);

}
```

Deleting nodes from an AVL tree relies on the same rotation operations that we previously discussed for insertion and is implemented in a similar fashion. We leave the implementation of item deletion as an exercise.

### 10.2 Red-Black Trees

AVL trees provide a great improvement to the basic binary search tree. Like many ADTs, the choice to use one over another depends on the shape of the data that we intend to store in the ADT and how they may or may not change over time.

The AVL tree imposed an additional balance property to guarantee O(log[2]N) performance on all operations despite any implicit ordering in the original data or in modifications incurred by insertions and deletions. The balance of an AVL tree is maintained with the application of additional rotation operations when the tree is modified.

Although the time cost to rebalance an AVL tree is hidden by the benefits in efficient search, applications that require constant changes to an AVL tree are still hindered by the overhead of the rotation operations. Is there an ADT that loosens the balancing property to reduce overhead but retains the search performance characteristics that we want? Fortunately, there is.

Red-Black trees are another implementation of binary search trees that provide O(log[2]N) efficiency by reducing the number of rotations, at the cost of a perfectly balanced tree. Although the balance of a Red-Black tree is not precisely maintained at all times, it is good enough to allow for guaranteed O(log[2]N) search time. For this reason, Red-Black trees are by far the most popular implementation strategy in practice. They are the basis for the implementation of the `Set` and `Map` ADT in C++’s standard template library and Java’s implementation of its `TreeMap` collection. They are used in many data structures in computational geometry, and found in the implementation of the task scheduler in the Linux operating system.

In addition to the constraints imposed on regular binary trees, Red-Black trees impose the following properties:

1.  A node in a Red-Black tree is labeled as either red or black.

2.  The root is labeled as black.

3.  All leaves that are `NULL` are labeled black.

4.  If a node is labeled red, then its two child nodes must be labeled black.

5.  Every path from a given node to a `NULL` node must have the same number of black nodes. This is called the [black-height](#bm01.xhtml_gloss023) of a Red-Black tree.

The coloring of `NULL` nodes as black is done for completeness and can make the implementation of Red-Black trees more clear. Note that it is only the red nodes that must have black children—black nodes may have either red or black children. [Figure 10.11](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) shows valid and invalid Red-Black trees, with black nodes colored blue and red nodes colored white.

![](Images/f10-11.jpg)

Figure 10.11 Valid/invalid Red-Black trees

[Figures 10.11a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) and [10.11b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) are not Red-Black trees because the number of black nodes from the root to a `NULL` are not the same. [Figure 10.11c](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) violates property 4, which requires all red nodes to have black children. [Figures 10.11d](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) and [10.11e](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig11) satisfy the Red-Black properties, and thus they are valid Red-Black trees.

#### Inserting into Red-Black Trees

Fortunately, the implementation of Red-Black trees does not require any significant changes to the operations previously described for standard binary search trees in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08). However, we will extend our definition of the binary search tree slightly to include in each node a pointer to its parent node, for reasons that we will discuss shortly.

To ensure that the properties for Red-Black trees are maintained, we must apply additional operations to correct the tree if violations are encountered. For AVL trees, we used only rotation to correct imbalance in the tree. Red-Black trees, on the other hand, try to recolor the tree, followed by rotation if that fails. That is, after a change to a Red-Black tree, we may violate the coloring rules. This in turn may require us to swap the colors of nearby nodes until we satisfy the rules. If recoloring doesn’t work, we must then resort to using AVL rotation operations. The recoloring operation is cheaper than performing rotations. The hope is that it will be applied in many cases, rather than just the more expensive rotation operations. For insertion, we use the following basic procedure:

1.  Insert a new node N and label it as red.

2.  Perform recoloring to maintain Red-Black tree properties.

3.  If recoloring fails to maintain the required properties, perform rotations.

![](Images/f10-12.jpg)

Figure 10.12 The family tree

To implement this procedure efficiently, as mentioned previously, it is helpful to extend our definition of the Binary Search Tree ADT to include a link to the parent of a given node. Doing so will allow us to navigate both down through the children of a node and up through its parent. However, it does require us to update the insertion and deletion methods in our standard binary search tree implementation to ensure that references are updated properly. This extension is necessary for implementing the algorithms for Red-Black trees. We leave its implementation as an exercise.

Inserting a node N into a Red-Black tree can best be described in relation to other nodes in the tree (in particular, the parent of N, the grandparent of N, and the uncle of N). The parent of N is clearly the node whose child is N. Likewise, the grandparent of N is naturally the parent of N’s parent. The uncle of N would then be the sibling node of N’s parent. An instance of this family tree can be seen in [Figure 10.12](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig12).

Now that we know who is related to whom, we can talk about the details of inserting nodes into a Red-Black tree.

As previously mentioned, a new node is inserted into a Red-Black tree just as it is into a traditional binary search tree. This insertion might cause one or more properties of a Red-Black tree to be violated. If this is the case, we must determine where the problem is and either recolor (if we can) or restructure through rotation. We can determine what to do based on the location of the node N being examined (initially the newly inserted node) and possibly the color of its parent node, its uncle node, or both. The following algorithm formalizes the approach:

First, if N is the root node, then its color must be black. In this scenario, N is either a newly created node, in which case its color starts out as red, or the node’s color is red because of a previous recoloring (as discussed next). In either case, we must recolor the node to black. This maintains the Red-Black tree properties, as we simply add 1 to the black-height of the already valid Red-Black tree.

![](Images/f10-13.jpg)

Figure 10.13 Recoloring after inserting N

Otherwise, if N is not the root node or the parent of N is not black, then what we do next depends on the color of N’s uncle. If N’s uncle is colored red, we will apply recoloring to maintain our Red-Black tree properties. In particular, we recolor N’s parent and uncle to black and change the grandparent of N to red. This ensures that we satisfy the Red-Black tree properties in the immediate vicinity of change with respect to N. However, our recoloring might have caused problems with the grandparent of N with respect to its parent and uncle, so we must perform further recoloring on the grandparent of N. This is a tail-recursive call to our `ReColoring` algorithm on N’s grandparent. See [Chapter 7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07) to recall the details of tail recursion to see why this is an efficient implementation.

The implications of inserting node N into a Red-Black tree when N is not the root and N’s parent and uncle are both labeled as red are shown in [Figure 10.13](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig13).

In the case where N is not the root, or N’s parent is not black and N’s uncle is black, we must work at restructuring the tree to maintain our Red-Black properties. Fortunately, we can leverage our understanding of rotation on AVL trees to manage Red-Black trees in the event that recoloring is not successful. Like the AVL tree, this breaks down into four cases when N’s uncle is black:

1.  If P is a left child of G and N is a left child of P, apply right rotation and swap the color of G and P.

2.  If P is a left child of G and N is a right child of P, apply left-right rotation and swap the color of G and N.

3.  If P is a right child of G and N is a right child of P, apply left rotation and swap the color of G and P.

4.  If P is a right child of G and N is a left child of P, apply right-left rotation and swap the color of G and N.

We can express these rules more formally in the following algorithm:

This algorithm is quite similar to the `Balance` algorithm that we discussed for AVL trees earlier in this chapter. However, which rotation procedure to apply is determined by the coloring of the nodes, rather than the balance factor, and the structure of the tree with respect to the node N. In addition, we perform recoloring of the nodes depending on which rotation is applied.

In [Figure 10.14](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig14), the rules for recoloring do not apply, as N is not the root node and its uncle is black. Thus, we must apply restructuring, which identifies the Left-Left case as the parent P is a child of G and N is the child of P. Thus, we right-rotate around G and swap the colors of G and P to satisfy the Red-Black tree properties. The Right-Right case is depicted in [Figure 10.16](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig16) and is the mirror image of the Left-Left case. [Figures 10.15](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig15) and [10.17](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig17) show the Left-Right and Right-Left cases, respectively. Both require a double rotation, followed by swapping the colors of G and N.

![](Images/f10-14.jpg)

Figure 10.14 Left-Left restructuring

![](Images/f10-15.jpg)

Figure 10.15 Left-Right restructuring

![](Images/f10-16.jpg)

Figure 10.16 Right-Right restructuring

#### Implementing Recoloring for Red-Black Trees

Although there is some additional overhead in managing Red-Black trees, the algorithms that we just presented are straightforward to implement in C++. We must be able to refer to the parent, grandparent, and uncle of a particular node and associate with each `TreeNode` either a red or black color. The latter is best implemented using C++’s `enum` type to represent each of these colors. The following C++ code would be a suitable way to extend the `TreeNode` type originally presented in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08):

![](Images/f10-17.jpg)

Figure 10.17 Right-Left restructuring

```
enum Color { RED, BLACK };

struct TreeNode

{

  ItemType info;

  Color color;

  TreeNode* left;

  TreeNode* right;

  TreeNode* parent;

};
```

We could easily use the `TreeNode` type as is; however, it would quickly become cumbersome to refer to the grandparent and uncle of a node using pointers alone. For example, to refer to the uncle of a node N, we would need to do something like this:

```
N->parent->parent->right
```

Not only is this lengthy to type, but we can’t tell if N’s parent is the right or left child of its parent. In this code fragment, we are assuming that it is the left. However, if this is not the case, then the uncle would be the left child of the grandparent. Furthermore, what happens if N is the root node or if it did not have a grandparent or an uncle? Clearly, we would need to be able to detect this and provide a sensible return value.

For these reasons, it makes sense to write helper routines that perform the proper error checking. We could refactor the code entirely and rewrite `TreeNode` as a class instead of a struct, but we will maintain backward compatibility with previous chapters and illustrate some of these helper routines as functions rather than methods of a class. The following C++ functions solidify this point:

```
TreeNode* Parent(TreeNode* N)

{

  return N->parent

}

TreeNode* GrandParent(TreeNode* N)

{

  TreeNode* P = Parent(N);

  if (P == NULL) return NULL;

  else return Parent(P);

}

TreeNode* Uncle(TreeNode* N)

{

  TreeNode* G = GrandParent(N);

  if (G == NULL) return NULL;

  else if (Parent(N) == G->left) return G->right;

  else return G->left;

}
```

To make things simple, our utility functions will return `NULL` if the requested family member does not exist. For example, `Parent` returns `NULL` if the parent node does not exist (we can also use this to identify a root node), `GrandParent` returns `NULL` if either the parent or the grandparent is `NULL` , and `Uncle` correctly identifies where the uncle node resides in the tree and returns `NULL` if any of the references is `NULL` along that path.

Now that we can safely refer to nodes that are important to our Red-Black tree algorithms, we may want to provide yet another helper function to set and retrieve the color of a given node. Remember that we had mentioned that treating `NULL` children as though they have the color black would simplify our algorithms. The `GetColor` function will return either the color of the given node or black if it is `NULL. SetColor` will set the color of a node if it is not `NULL` . Here are the C++ function definitions:

```
Color GetColor(TreeNode* N)

{

  if (N == NULL) return BLACK;

  else return N->color;

}

void SetColor(TreeNode* N, Color color)

{

  if (N != NULL) N->color = color;

}
```

These additional functions help us keep the Red-Black tree algorithms clear and easier to maintain and debug. Now we are in a good position to implement the recoloring algorithm:

```
void ReColor(TreeNode* N)

{

  if (N == NULL) return; // do nothing if N is NULL

  TreeNode* P = Parent(N);

  TreeNode* G = GrandParent(N);

  TreeNode* U = Uncle(N);

  if (P == NULL) N->color = BLACK; // N is the root node

  else if (P != NULL || GetColor(P) != BLACK) {

    if (GetColor(U) == RED) {

      SetColor(P, BLACK);

      SetColor(U, BLACK);

      SetColor(G, RED);

      ReColor(G);

    }

    else

      ReStructure(N);

}
```

The algorithm for recoloring falls out naturally from the helper functions that we have defined here. First, we check if the node N provided as an argument to `ReColor` is NULL. If it is, there is nothing more to be done, so we simply return from the function. If N is the root node, we color it black; otherwise, if N is not the root node or N’s parent is not colored black, we either recolor if N’s uncle is red or restructure if N’s uncle is black. The C++ implementation for `ReStructure` relies on our previous rotation operations for AVL trees (as discussed in [Section 10.1](#ch10.xhtml_ch10lev1sec1), earlier in this chapter) and the helper routines we have illustrated in this discussion. We leave its implementation as an exercise.

Weaving the `ReColor` procedure into the standard binary search tree implementation for `PutItem` is clean and simple. Unlike our AVL implementation, which required calls to the `Balance` function after each recursive call to the `Insert` operation, `ReColor` can easily be invoked once after `TreeNode` is created. Notice that we changed the signature of `Insert` slightly to include a reference to the parent node so we can initialize the new `TreeNode` with its proper parent. The following highlighted extensions to `Insert` and `PutItem` are the only changes required to maintain the properties of a Red-Black tree during insertion:

```
void Insert(TreeNode*& tree, TreeNode* parent, ItemType item)

// Inserts item into tree.

// Post: item is in tree; search property is maintained.

{

  if (tree == NULL)

  {// Insertion place found. 

   tree = new TreeNode;

   tree->right = NULL;

   tree->left = NULL;

   tree->parent = parent;

   tree->info = item;

   ReColor(tree);

 }

 else if (item < tree->info)

   Insert(tree->left, tree, item);       // Insert in left subtree.

  else

    Insert(tree->right, tree, item);      // Insert in right subtree.

}

void TreeType::PutItem(ItemType item)

// Calls the recursive function Insert to insert item into tree.

{

  Insert(root, NULL, item);

}
```

The main Red-Black tree property violation that occurs during item insertion is two consecutive red nodes along a path in the tree. As has been demonstrated, the combination of recoloring and restructuring can easily fix the problem. With node deletion, however, the black-height property of a Red-Black tree can be violated. Recall that the black-height property of a Red-Black tree dictates that the number of black nodes along every path from the root to its leaves must be the same. If a black node is deleted, the number of black nodes along the path that contained that node will change, causing the black-height property to be violated. Unfortunately, the deletion for Red-Black trees is substantially more complicated than insertion. We leave the details of this process to an advanced textbook on data structures.

#### Red-Black Tree Summary

Red-Black trees trade off a perfectly balanced tree (as with AVL trees) for a mostly balanced tree that is faster to maintain. In practice, this tradeoff is a good one. The balancing of the tree is not perfect, but it is enough to guarantee O(log[2]N) search performance. For this reason, the standard libraries for many programming languages (including C++) and internal data structures in modern operating systems use Red-Black trees in their implementation. Again, the decision to use one implementation of an ADT over another is highly dependent on the problem that you are trying to solve and the nature of the data that you are storing in the data structure. As you saw in our implementation of both AVL trees and Red-Black trees, the interface for the standard binary search tree was consistently maintained. This allows the client of the tree ADT to easily swap out one implementation for another with little impact on the surrounding code. A consistent interface is an excellent example of software engineering at its best.

### 10.3 B-Trees

In the chapter on binary search trees ([Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)) and the previous two sections of this chapter, the focus has been on trees that have nodes containing a single data item (info) and no more than two children. Is it possible to have trees with more than two children and possibly more data items within a single node? The answer to this question is yes. In this section, we provide a brief overview of the B-tree ADT, a generalization of the binary search tree that may have up to m ≥ 2 children and k – 1 data items, where k is the number of children and k ≤ m.

Similar to the AVL trees and Red-Black binary search trees, B-trees are self-balancing trees that provide operations (e.g., search, insert, and delete) exhibiting logarithmic time efficiency. To ensure this performance, B-trees of order m must adhere to the following properties:

1.  Each node must have at most m children.

2.  Each internal node has at least [m/2] children.

3.  The root node must have at least 2 children if it is not a leaf.

4.  A nonleaf node with k children must have k – 1 data items (keys).

5.  All leaves must appear at the same level in the tree.

Binary search trees can be considered an instance of a B-tree of order 2 if all the leaves appear at the same level and the root node has at least 2 children (if the root is not a leaf). Because B-trees may have several keys at each node, and all leaves must appear at the same level, they are typically broad, or bushy, rather than deep as is often the case for binary search trees. [Figure 10.18](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18) shows examples of B-trees of order 2 and order 5\. We diverge slightly from our previous figures that illustrate trees to show the existence of multiple child links within a single node. Furthermore, we show child links between data items to make the relationship between data items and the values stored in their subtrees more clear. What this relationship is will be elaborated on shortly.

[Figure 10.18a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18) shows a B-tree of order 2, also known as a binary search tree. This is a valid B-tree, as it satisfies each of the properties we have talked about in this chapter. Each node has at most 2 children, each internal node has at least [2/2] or 0 children, the root node has at least 2 children, each nonleaf node with 2 children has 1 data item, and all leaves appear at the same level. Since this is a standard binary search tree, the explicit representation of the link fields in the figure are unnecessary.

![](Images/f10-18.jpg)

Figure 10.18 B-tree examples

Likewise, [Figure 10.18b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18) is a valid B-tree of order 5 that satisfies these properties. It satisfies property 1 because each node has no more than 5 children. We do not have any internal nodes in this example, so property 2 is trivially satisfied. If we did have internal nodes, then each one must have at least [5/2] (ceiling) or 3 children. The only nonleaf node we have in this tree is the root, which has 3 children and 2 keys, so property 4 is fulfilled. Finally, all leaves appear at the same level. We show the explicit link fields here to make it clear between which data items a link occurs.

Searching a B-tree is accomplished in the same way as the standard binary search tree. As you can see in [Figure 10.18a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18), all data items, or keys, that are less than a given node’s key reside in its left subtree, and all keys that are greater go into its right subtree. Of course, if the data item equals the key in the node being examined, then we have found the element we are looking for.

The B-tree of order 5 in [Figure 10.18b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18) requires more comparison checks, as each node may contain at most 4 keys, k[1] – k[4], from left to right. In particular, if we are searching for a data item whose key is d and d is not found in the node being examined, we must compare d to each of the keys k[1] through k[m – 1] (where m is the maximum number of children a node may have for a B-tree of order m) to determine which subtree we must search. If d < k[1], then we must search the leftmost subtree. Likewise, if d > k[m][-1], then we must search the right-most subtree. Otherwise, for each key i ≥ 2 < m, we determine if k[i] < d < k[i+1] and search the subtree between k[i] and k[i][+][1]. For example, if we are searching for the element whose key is 21 in the B-tree of order 5 in [Figure 10.18b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18), we would start at the root node comparing each of the keys in turn. In this instance, 21 is not less than 10, so the element we are looking for will not be found in its leftmost subtree. However, 21 is greater than 10 and less than 30, so we would traverse the tree between those two keys. Applying the same procedure to this subtree would yield success, as 21 is the third key in the root of that subtree.

Like the other self-balancing search trees we have discussed, modifications to the tree (e.g., insertion and deletion) require additional work to ensure that its properties are maintained. This is no different for B-trees; however, the work involved is slightly more complicated than the self-balancing binary search trees. Here, we present a high-level algorithm for B-tree insertion:

![](Images/f10-19.jpg)

Figure 10.19 B-tree insertion

The most notable difference between this algorithm and other insertion algorithms that we have covered in this chapter is the deletion and creation of new nodes through splitting and the reassignment of elements to other nodes when we don’t have room for the element that we are trying to insert. In [Figure 10.19](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig19), we demonstrate the insertion of the value 6 into the B-tree shown in [Figure 10.18b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig18).

First, we attempt to insert 6 into the root, as shown in [Figure 10.19a](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig19). Because 6 is less than 10, we look to insert it into the left subtree. The leaf node in the left subtree is full, so we must perform splitting to accommodate the insertion. We split the node into two equal parts, as shown in [Figure 10.19b](#ch10.xhtml_ch10fig19), create two new nodes, and remove the original after copying the keys from both parts into the appropriate nodes. The new element, 6, happens to be the middle element, so we insert it into the parent node in ascending order. This requires us to shift the existing elements, 10 and 30, to the right and place 6 in the first slot. Finally, we adjust the child pointers appropriately so that they now refer to the newly created nodes.

B-trees are a generalization of the self-balancing binary search tree. Like all the ADTs we have explored, the choice to use a B-tree depends on the application. Although all tree ADTs can be saved and restored from disk, B-trees happen to be very well suited for doing this. Disks are designed to read and write blocks of values more efficiently than individual values. Because each B-tree node is likely to contain many elements, it is a good match for this inherent nature of disk access.

Making disk access fast becomes important when the application must maintain trees that are larger than the available memory. For this reason, B-trees are often used to implement database systems and file systems that are likely to store terabytes of data.

In practice, users of a database rarely need to operate on all the data at the same time. The data that are not in active use can be saved to disk until they are needed. In such an application, the order of the B-tree will typically be related to the size of the disk input/output (I/O) blocks to maximize the efficiency of the hardware.

### Summary

In this chapter, we introduced three self-balancing tree ADTs to ensure O(log[2]N) guaranteed search efficiency. We explained when and why you might use each of these trees, depending on the nature of your application and its data. We covered the AVL tree, which maintains balance across insertion and deletion operations using four rotation operations. These rotation operations are applied based on the structure of the tree after it is modified. The AVL tree, along with its rotation operations, provides logarithmic search performance at the expense of fixing the tree during insertion and deletion.

We also discussed the Red-Black tree, which introduced a recoloring procedure along with the four AVL rotation operations to reduce the amount of work required to ensure O(log[2]N) search performance. Although the recoloring algorithm does not always result in a balanced tree, it is good enough to give us the guaranteed performance that we require for searching.

Finally, we explored the B-tree, a generalization of a binary search tree that may have a maximum of m children per node. The most distinguishing feature of the B-tree is the splitting operation, which is used to ensure that all leaf nodes are at the same level in the tree.
