//       values[leftFirst]..values[rightLast] are now sorted.

{

  int index = leftFirst;

  int saveFirst = leftFirst;

  while ((leftFirst <= leftLast) && (rightFirst <= rightLast))

  {

    if (values[leftFirst] < values[rightFirst])

    {

      tempArray[index] = values[leftFirst];

      leftFirst++;

    }

    else

    {

      tempArray[index] = values[rightFirst];

      rightFirst++;

    }

    index++;

  }

  while (leftFirst <= leftLast)

  // Copy remaining items from left half.

  {

    tempArray[index] = values[leftFirst];

    leftFirst++;

    index++;

  }

  while (rightFirst <= rightLast)

  // Copy remaining items from right half.

  {

    tempArray[index] = values[rightFirst];

    rightFirst++;

    index++;

  }

  for (index = saveFirst; index <= rightLast; index++)

    values[index] = tempArray[index];

}
```

Note that we are using `tempArray` much like a queue in this function, and that would be an alternate approach to the implementation. If we use a queue ADT that is built on a dynamic linked list, then we could avoid the need for passing `tempArray` as a parameter. However, in this case, we chose a self-contained implementation to keep the code simple.

#### The `MergeSort` Function

As we have said, most of the work takes place in the merge task. The actual `MergeSort` function is short and simple. Before we code it, however, we want to revisit an aspect of using template functions. Recall that a template function declaration doesn’t actually define a function. The function must be instantiated with a concrete type before it can be used. In many cases, the C++ compiler can infer the type of the function that is intended from the way it is called and automatically instantiate it. However, we can also specify the type explicitly in the call by writing it in angle braces after the function name. In [Section 12.8](#ch12.xhtml_ch12lev1sec8), we will revisit `MergeSort` and encounter a reason to use explicit instantiation. Here, though, we show how that is done:

```
template<class ItemType>

void MergeSort(ItemType values[], int first, int last. ItemType tempArray)

// Post: The elements in values are sorted by key.

{

  if (first < last)

  {

    int middle = (first + last) / 2;

    MergeSort<ItemType>(values, first, middle, tempArray);

    MergeSort<ItemType>(values, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

    Merge<ItemType>(values, first, middle, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

  }

}
```

##### Analyzing the Merge Sort

The `MergeSort` function splits the original array into two halves. First, it sorts the first half of the array, using the divide-and-conquer approach; then it sorts the second half of the array using the same approach; finally, it merges the two halves. To sort the first half of the array, it follows the same approach, splitting and merging. During the sorting process, the splitting and merging operations are intermingled. To simplify the analysis, however, we imagine that all the splitting occurs first. We can view the process in this way without affecting the correctness of the algorithm.

We view the `MergeSort` algorithm as continually dividing the original array (of size N) in two, until it has created N one-element subarrays. [Figure 12.11](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig11) shows this point of view for an array with an original size of 16\. The total work needed to divide the array in half, over and over again, until we reach subarrays of size 1, is O(N). After all, we end up with N subarrays of size 1.

Each subarray of size 1 is obviously a sorted subarray. To merge two sorted subarrays of size X and size Y into a single sorted subarray using the `Merge` operation requires O(X + Y) steps. We can see this fact because each time through the while loops of the `Merge` function, we advance either the `leftFirst` index or the `rightFirst` index by 1. Because we stop processing when these indexes become greater than their last counterparts, we know that we take a total of `(leftLast – leftFirst + 1) + (rightLast –` `rightFirst + 1)` steps. This expression represents the sum of the lengths of the two subarrays being processed.

How many times is the `Merge` function called? And what are the sizes of the subarrays involved? Let’s work from the bottom up. The original array of size N is eventually split into N subarrays of size 1\. Merging two of those subarrays into a subarray of size 2 requires O(1 + 1) = O(2) steps based on the analysis given in the preceding paragraph. That is, we must perform this merge operation a total of N/2 times (we have N one-element subarrays, and we are merging them two at a time). Thus, the total number of steps to create all the sorted two-element subarrays is O(N).

![](Images/f12-11.jpg)

Figure 12.11 Analysis of the function `MergeSort` with N = 16

We repeat this process to create four-element subarrays. It takes four steps to merge two two-element subarrays. We must perform this merge operation a total of N/4 times (we have N/2 two-element subarrays, and we are merging them two at a time). The total number of steps to create all of the sorted four-element subarrays is O(N) (4 * N/4 = N).

The same reasoning leads us to conclude that each of the other levels of merging also requires O(N) steps. At each level, the sizes of the subarrays double, but the number of subarrays is cut in half, which balances out.

We now know that it takes a total of O(N) steps to perform merging at each level of merging. How many levels are there? The number of levels of merging is equal to the number of times that we can split the original array in half. If the original array is size N, we have log[2]N levels (this is just like the analysis of the binary search algorithm). For example, in [Figure 12.11](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig11), the size of the original array is 16 and the number of levels of merging is 4\. Because we have log[2]N levels, and we require N steps at each level, the total cost of the merge operation is O(Nlog[2]N). Because the splitting phase was only O(N), we conclude that `MergeSort` has O(Nlog[2]N) complexity. [Table 12.2](#ch12.xhtml_ch12table2) illustrates that for large values of N, O(Nlog[2]N) represents a big improvement over O(N²).

The disadvantage of `MergeSort` derives from the fact that it requires an auxiliary array that is as large as the original array to be sorted. If the array is large and space is a critical factor, this sort may not be an appropriate choice. Next, we discuss two sorts that move elements within the original array and do not need an auxiliary array.

| N | log[2]N | N[2] | N log[2]N |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 32 | 5 | 1,024 | 160 |
| 64 | 6 | 4,096 | 384 |
| 128 | 7 | 16,384 | 896 |
| 256 | 8 | 65,536 | 2,048 |
| 512 | 9 | 262,144 | 4,608 |
| 1024 | 10 | 1,048,576 | 10,240 |
| 2048 | 11 | 4,194,304 | 22,528 |
| 4096 | 12 | 16,777,216 | 49,152 |

Table 12.2 Comparing N² and N log[2]N

#### Quick Sort

Recall from [Chapter 7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07) that `QuickSort` is another recursive divide-and-conquer sort. At each stage of the algorithm, we identify a split point value, then move all values less than or equal to the value into the first part of the array, leaving those that are greater in the remaining portion of the array. The two sections of the array are not yet sorted, but we can call `QuickSort` to sort each of them so the process recursively repeats until we reach the trivial case of a single-element array.

The analysis of `QuickSort` is very similar to that of `MergeSort`. On the first call, every element in the array is compared to the dividing value (the “split value”), so the work done is O(N). The array is divided into two parts (not necessarily halves), which are then examined. Each of these pieces is then divided in two, and so on. If each piece is split approximately in half, O(log[2]N) splits occur. At each split, we make O(N) comparisons. Thus, `QuickSort` is also an O(Nlog[2]N) algorithm, which is quicker than the O(N²) sorts discussed earlier in this chapter.

But `QuickSort` isn’t always quicker. Note that log[2]N splits take place if each split divides the segment of the array approximately in half. As we’ve seen, `QuickSort` is sensitive to the order of the data.

What happens if the array is already sorted when we call our first version of `QuickSort`? The splits are very lopsided, and the subsequent recursive calls to `QuickSort` break into a segment of one element and a segment containing all the rest of the array. This situation produces a sort that is not at all quick. In fact, N – 1 splits occur; in this case, `QuickSort` has O(N²) complexity.

Such a situation is very unlikely to arise by chance. By way of analogy, consider the odds of shuffling a deck of cards and coming up with a sorted deck. On the other hand, in some applications, you may know that the original array is likely to be sorted or nearly sorted. In such cases, you would want to use either a different splitting algorithm or a different sort—maybe even `ShortBubble`.

What about space requirements? `QuickSort` does not require an extra array, as `MergeSort` does. Does it have any extra space requirements, besides the few local variables? Yes—remember that `QuickSort` uses a recursive approach. Many levels of recursion can be “saved” on the system stack at any time. On average, the algorithm requires O(log[2]N) extra space to hold this information, and in the worst case, it requires O(N) extra space—the same as `MergeSort`.

#### Heap Sort

In [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09) we looked at `HeapSort`, another O(log[2]N) sort. Recall that at the logical level, a heap is a binary tree with two special properties: the shape property, where the tree is complete, and the order property, where the value stored in every node is greater than or equal to the value in each of its children.

We saw that at the implementation level, it is possible to take an array and convert it to a heap using `ReheapDown` on successively smaller portions of the array. Then we sort the heap by swapping the root (the first array element) with the value in its proper position (at the end of the unsorted portion), decreasing the size of the heap by one, and reheaping the remaining elements. The process repeats until there is just one element left in the unsorted portion.

##### Analyzing the Heap Sort

The code for `HeapSort` is very short—only a few lines of code plus the utility function `ReheapDown`. These few lines of code, however, do quite a bit. All the elements in the original array are rearranged to satisfy the order property of heaps, moving the largest element up to the top of the array, only to put it immediately into its place at the bottom.

For small arrays, `HeapSort` is not very efficient because of its overhead. For large arrays, however, `HeapSort` is very efficient. Consider the sorting loop. We loop through N – 1 times, swapping elements and reheaping. The comparisons occur in `ReheapDown`. A complete binary tree with N nodes has O(log[2](N + 1)) levels. In the worst case, then, if the root element has to be bumped down to a leaf position, the `ReheapDown` function would make O(log[2]N) comparisons; the function `ReheapDown` is O(log[2]N). Multiplying this activity by N – 1 iterations, O(N), shows that the sorting loop is O(Nlog[2]N).

But what about the cost of the original heap-building operation? That is indeed an additional O(N) operations. But because O(Nlog[2]N) dominates the time as N becomes large, the work done by `HeapSort` is still just proportional to O(Nlog[2]N) comparisons. Note that, unlike `QuickSort`, `HeapSort`’s efficiency is not affected by the initial order of the elements. `HeapSort` is just as efficient in terms of space; it uses only one array to store the data.

#### Testing

We have examined several sorting algorithms: selection sort, two versions of bubble sort, insertion sort, merge sort, quick sort, and heap sort. Before we examine other issues involved in sorting, we need to verify that our algorithms are correct. We can use the same pattern that we have used for earlier ADTs: We can take as input the name of a sorting algorithm, apply that algorithm to an array of values, and print the results. We need to initialize an array with random numbers, refresh the array after it has been sorted, and generate an array of new values.

On the Web, the file `SortDr.cpp` contains the test driver. The file `Sorts.in` contains a test plan that generates an array, applies each of the algorithms to it, generates a second array, and applies one of the algorithms. `Sorts.out` holds the output from the driver, and `Sorts.screen` holds what was written on the screen. Examine these files carefully. Be sure that you understand them. You are asked to design a more involved test plan in the exercises.

### 12.6 Efficiency and Other Considerations

Throughout this chapter, we have based our analysis of efficiency on the number of comparisons made by a sorting algorithm. The Big-O analyses that we have done for this operation are one indicator of the processing time that one algorithm takes relative to another as the number of items becomes large. But in practice, there are other considerations that affect our choice of algorithm and the details of its implementation. In this section, we take a closer look at these other factors.

#### When N Is Small

The number of comparisons done by a sort gives a rough estimate of the computation time involved. The other activities that accompany the comparison (swapping, keeping track of Boolean flags, and so forth) contribute to the constant of proportionality of the algorithm. In comparing Big-O evaluations, we ignored constants and smaller-order terms because we wanted to know how the algorithm would perform for large values of N. In general, an O(N²) sort requires few extra activities in addition to the comparisons, so its constant of proportionality is fairly small. On the other hand, an O(Nlog[2]N) sort may be more complex, with more overhead and thus a larger constant of proportionality. This situation may cause anomalies in the relative performances of the algorithms when the value of N is small. In such a case, N² is not much greater than Nlog[2]N, and the constants may dominate instead, causing an O(N²) sort to run faster than an O(Nlog[2]N) sort.

We have discussed sorting algorithms that have a complexity of either O(N²) or O(Nlog[2]N). The obvious question is: Are some algorithms better than O(Nlog[2]N)? No—it has been proven theoretically that we cannot do better than O(Nlog[2]N) for sorting algorithms that are based on comparing keys.

#### Eliminating Calls to Functions

At the beginning of this chapter, we mentioned that it may be desirable, for efficiency reasons, to streamline the code as much as possible, even at the expense of readability. In some cases, though, we can have both. For instance, we have consistently written

```
Swap(item1, item2)
```

with the function defined using the `inline` specifier instead of the corresponding inline expansion:

```
tempItem = item1; item1 = item2; item2 = tempItem;
```

In `SelectionSort`, we coded the operation to find the minimum element as a function, `MinIndex`; in `BubbleSort`, we coded a function `BubbleUp`. Coding such operations as functions made the code simpler to write and to understand, avoiding a more complicated nested loop structure.

Although the function calls are clearer, in the actual coding, it may be better to use the `inline` specifier, or even to code the function body directly if the compiler doesn’t take the hint. Function calls require extra overhead that you may prefer to avoid in a sort, where these routines are called many times.

The recursive sorting functions, `MergeSort` and `QuickSort`, lead to a similar situation: They require the extra overhead involved in executing recursive calls. You may want to avoid this overhead by writing nonrecursive versions of these functions.

#### Programmer Time

If the recursive calls are less efficient, why would anyone ever decide to use a recursive version of a sort? The decision involves a choice between types of efficiency. Until now, we have been concerned only with minimizing computer time. While computers become faster and cheaper over time, it is not clear that computer programmers are following that trend. In some situations, programmer time may be an important consideration in choosing a sort algorithm and its implementation. In this respect, the recursive version of `QuickSort` is more desirable than its nonrecursive counterpart, which requires the programmer to simulate the recursion explicitly. Doing so is more likely to introduce errors that take even more programming effort to resolve. Fortunately, for sorting large amounts of data, we can often rely on existing packages, such as the C++ STL, that contain highly optimized and thoroughly debugged sorting operations.

#### Space Considerations

As we have seen, memory space is also an efficiency consideration. Memory space is not a very important factor in choosing a sorting algorithm to sort a small amount of data. But as N grows large, it can have a much greater impact. With `MergeSort`, the space used was double the amount needed for the items being sorted, and there was overhead for the recursive calls. With `QuickSort`, the elements are sorted within the original array, but in the worst case, the recursion can push approximately N sets of parameters and local variables onto the run-time stack. If the items being sorted are similar in size to what is pushed on the stack for each call, then the space could again be doubled.

Our `HeapSort` algorithm also uses recursion, but only in the `ReheapDown` function, which keeps the tree perfectly balanced. Thus, at any given time, at most log[2](N) calls are pushed on the run-time stack. No extra space is needed to store the array values, other than in swapping them. Thus, `HeapSort` is efficient for both time and space.

Does this mean that you should always use `HeapSort`? If you have a large amount of data, it is indeed one of the better choices. But its complexity means that for smaller amounts of data, it may take longer than a simpler O(N²) sort that also avoids the space overhead of recursion. In the next section, we see another aspect of sorting that might cause us to choose a sorting algorithm other than `HeapSort`.

#### Keys and Stability

In our descriptions of the various sorts, we showed examples of sorting arrays using unique keys. A record may also contain secondary keys, which may or may not be unique. For instance, a student record may contain the following data members:

![](Images/f0698-01.gif)

If the data elements are only single integers, it doesn’t matter whether you maintain the original order of duplicate values. However, preserving the original order of records with identical key values may be desirable. If a sort preserves this order, it is said to be a [stable sort](#bm01.xhtml_gloss133).

Suppose that the items on our array are student records with the following declarations:

```
struct AddressType

{

   .

   .

   .

   StrType city;

   long zip;

};

struct NameType

{

   StrType firstName;

   StrType lastName;

};

struct PersonType

{

   long studentNumber;

   NameType name;

   AddressType address;

};
```

The list may normally be sorted by the unique key `studentNumber`. For some purposes, we might want to see a listing in order by name. In this case, the sort key would consist of the `name` data member. To sort by ZIP code, we would sort on the `address.zip` data member.

If the sort is stable, we can get a listing by ZIP code, with the names in alphabetical order within each ZIP code, by sorting twice: the first time by name and the second time by ZIP code. A stable sort preserves the order of the records when a match on the key is found. The second sort, by ZIP code, produces many such matches, but it preserves the alphabetical order imposed by the first sort.

To get a listing by city, with the ZIP codes in order within each city and the names alphabetically sorted within each ZIP code, we would sort three times, on the following keys:

```
name

address.zip

address.city
```

The file first would be put into alphabetical order by name. The output from the first sort would serve as input to a sort on ZIP code. The output from this sort would serve as input to a sort on city name. If the sorting algorithms used were stable, the final sort would give us the desired result.

Of the sorts that we have discussed in this book, only `HeapSort` is inherently unstable. The stability of the other sorts depends on how the code manages duplicate values. In the exercises, you are asked to examine the code for the other sorts as we have coded them and determine whether they are stable.

#### Sorting with Pointers

Sorting large records using some kind of sort that swaps the contents of two places may require a lot of computer time just to move sections of memory from one place to another every time we make a swap. We can reduce this move time by setting up an array of pointers to the records, and then rearranging the pointers instead of the actual records. [Figure 12.12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig12) illustrates this scheme. After the sort, the records are still in the same physical arrangement, but they may be accessed in order through the rearranged array of pointers.

![](Images/f12-12.jpg)

Figure 12.12 Sorting arrays with pointers

We may extend this scheme to keep a large array of data sorted on more than one key. The data can be physically stored according to the primary key, and auxiliary arrays can contain pointers to the same data but be sorted on secondary keys.

#### Caching

In our algorithms, we have treated memory as a uniform resource for storing data values. But not all computer memory is created equal. Storage cells are physical devices that store electrical charge. They are extremely small, so as to be packed densely on integrated circuits. Thus, they contain tiny amounts of charge. Reading data from them takes time because the circuitry must first be prepared so that the charge in the cell can be distinguished from the charge on the wires of the circuits. Next, the charge must be amplified repeatedly to make it large enough to work with. Even then, the retrieved value may be erroneous, so it passes through additional circuitry to correct errors. Reading out the charge empties the cell, so the value must then be written back into it. Finally, the value is given to the computer for processing.

It takes about as much time to access a memory cell as for the computer to execute 100 instructions. Recall that instructions are also stored in memory. Computers would be far slower if they had to wait around, figuratively drumming their fingers 100 times before getting each instruction from memory, and then have to wait again for the data to be read out for processing by that instruction.

The solution is to supply the computer with another, smaller memory, called a cache, that uses larger, faster cells. Recently used data and instructions are kept in the cache, where they can be accessed as quickly as the computer executes instructions.

The memory system also tries to predict ahead of time the memory locations that we’ll use. When a program accesses the values in an array in order, it starts running ahead of the program, pulling elements into cache before they are needed. The result is that most of the delay is hidden, so it appears the memory is keeping up.

There are, however, things a program can do that prevent the cache from hiding the cost of accessing main memory. One is accessing memory locations in an unpredictable pattern. Thus, we might find that `ShortBubble`, with its highly predictable access pattern, outperforms the less predictable `HeapSort` for a larger data set than our theoretical analysis would indicate.

When we sort using an array of pointers to objects, the objects can be stored in scattered locations in memory. Thus, the memory system can’t predict the location of the next object we will examine, so the program may have to wait for it to be moved from main memory to cache. Sorting a linked list suffers a similar problem because the nodes are only logically, not physically, in order in memory. When we relocate them in the list, we don’t move them to adjacent memory locations. We only change the pointer values to indicate a new logical relationship.

The point of this section is to give you an appreciation for the limitations of relying solely on theoretical analyses of the amount of work a sort does and the amount of space it needs in choosing which one to use. Depending on the application and the size of the data set, additional factors must be carefully considered. Performance tuning can involve quite a bit of experimentation and measurement.

### 12.7 Radix Sort

We have placed the radix sort in a section by itself for two reasons.

First, the radix sort is not a comparison sort; that is, the algorithm does not compare two items in a list. Therefore, we cannot analyze the amount of work done in terms of comparisons. In fact, the only thing that the radix sort has in common with the other sorts is that it takes an unsorted list as input and returns a sorted list as output.

Second, the radix sort is to sorting as hashing is to searching. That is, it uses the values in the individual keys to relocate items just as hashing uses the key values to determine where to place items. As in the other sorting algorithms, the parameters are the number of values to be sorted and the array that holds them.

The idea behind the radix sort is to divide the values to be sorted into as many subgroups as there are possible alternatives for each position in the key. For example, if the key is an integer number, each position is a digit and has 10 possibilities: 0 . . 9\. If the key is a string of letters and case is not important, then each position has 26 possibilities: a . . z. The number of possibilities is called the [radix](#bm01.xhtml_gloss110). After subdividing the values into radix subgroups, we combine them again into one array and repeat the process. If we begin with the least significant position in the key, regroup the values in order, and repeat the process as many times as there are positions in the key, moving one position to the left each time, the array will be sorted when we finish.

One way to think of the radix sort is that we are breaking each key into multiple subkeys, then using a series of stable sorts on each of the subkeys. Our stable sorting technique is based on the principle of hashing by the subkey value, so it is very fast.

Let’s illustrate this algorithm by sorting three-digit positive integers. Within a three-digit number, let’s refer to the ones, tens, and hundreds positions as positions 1, 2, and 3, respectively. We divide the values into ten subgroups based on the digit in the ones position (position 1). Let’s create an array of queues, `queues[0]..queues[9]`, to hold the groups. All items with 0 in the ones position are enqueued into `queues[0]`, all items with a 1 in the ones position are enqueued into `queues[1]`, and so on. As you can see, we are using the digit as an index (a trivial hash function) to indicate the corresponding queue where we insert the value.

After the first pass through the array, we collect the subgroups (queues) with the `queues[0]` subgroup on top and the `queues[9]` subgroup on the bottom. This collection process preserves the ordering that we have achieved, so it is effectively a stable sort on the given digit.

We repeat the process using the tens position and the hundreds position. When we collect the queues the last time, the values in the array are in order. This algorithm is illustrated in [Figures 12.13](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig13) and [12.14](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig14).

Look at the array after each pass; the digits in the position that corresponds to the pass number are sorted ([Figure 12.13](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig13)). Likewise, the digits in the pass-number position are the same as the index of the queue that it is in ([Figure 12.14](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig14)).

![](Images/f12-13.jpg)

Figure 12.13 Array after each pass

![](Images/f12-14.jpg)

Figure 12.14 Queues after each pass

Let’s first write the algorithm for the radix sort that matches our example and then examine ways to make it more general:

In this algorithm, each iteration of the outer loop corresponds to one pass in [Figures 12.13](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig13) and [12.14](#ch12.xhtml_ch12fig14). In the first pass, we use the ones digit of an integer item to determine the appropriate queue for the item. In the second pass, we use the tens digit. In the third pass, we use the hundreds digit. Next, we need to write the Collect Queues step of the algorithm. Here, we collect the items from all the queues and put them back into the `values` array:

Now that we understand the algorithm for three-digit integer keys, let’s look at how we can make it more general before we code it. When we examined the insertion of an item into a sorted list in [Chapter 3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03), we required the comparison of two items to be a member function of `ItemType`. The corresponding idea here is to make accessing the correct position in the key become a function. For example, with an integer key, we must extract the digits using `/` and `%`. If the key is a string, then we need access to an array of characters. The point is that only the user knows, so the user should provide a member function for `ItemType` to access successive positions in the key. This function (`SubKey`) takes the position number as a parameter.

The radix sort function itself, however, must know the number of positions in the key (`numPositions`) and the number of possible values for each position in the key (`radix`). We make `numPositions` and `radix` be parameters to the function:

```
template<class ItemType>

void RadixSort(ItemType values[], int numValues, int numPositions, int radix)

// Post: Elements in values are in order by key.

{

  QueType<ItemType> queues[radix];

  // With default constructor, each queue size is 500\. int whichQueue;

  for (int position = 1; position <= numPositions; position++)

  {

    for (int counter = 0; counter < length; counter++)

    {

      whichQueue = values[counter].SubKey(position);

      queues[whichQueue].Enqueue(values[counter]);

    }

    CollectQueues(values, queues, radix);

  }

}

template<class ItemType>

void CollectQueues(ItemType values[], QueType<ItemType> queues[],

     int radix)

// Post: queues are concatenated with queue[0]'s on top and

//       queue[9]'s on the bottom and copied into values.

{

  int index = 0; ItemType item;

  for (int counter = 0; counter < radix; counter++)

  {

    while (!queues[counter].IsEmpty())

    {

      queues[counter].Dequeue(item);

      values[index] = item;

      index++;

    }

  }

}
```

If the keys are integer values, then the function `SubKey` must take the position number and extract the digit in that position. Let’s calculate a few positions and look for a pattern. Assume that `itemKey` is the four-digit integer 8749:

| Position is 1: `itemKey % 10` | = 9 |
| Position is 2: `(itemKey / 10) % 10` | = 4 |
| Position is 3: `(itemKey / 100) % 10` | = 7 |
| Position is 4: `(itemKey / 1000) % 10` | = 8 |

Notice that as the position number gets larger, the second operand of the `/` operation increases. If we rewrite the first calculation as

Position is 1: `(itemKey / 1) % 10`

the pattern becomes even clearer:

> Result = (itemKey / 10^(position - 1)) % 10

If the key is alphabetic, then `SubKey` must take each character and convert it to a number between 0 and 25 (if case does not count) or between 0 and 51 (if case does matter).

#### Analyzing the Radix Sort

The amount of work done by the radix sort is more complicated than any scenario that we have examined so far. Each item in the array is processed `numPositions` times, making the Big-O analysis a function of two variables: N (the number of items to be sorted) and P (the number of positions in the key). The processing includes extracting a value from the key, inserting the item into a queue, dequeueing each item, and copying each item back into the array. We know that each operation is O(1), so an approximation is O(N * P). However, when N is large, it dominates P. (N is the elephant and P is the goldfish, to use our familiar analogy.)

In each iteration of the radix sort, the queues are collected, meaning that each item to be sorted is processed twice on each iteration: once to put it into a queue, and once when the queues are collected. We could streamline the processing in the radix sort somewhat by using the linked queue implementation and accessing the queues directly to re-create the intermediate list in linked form. However, this approach would require copying the final linked version back into the array-based form.

What about space requirements? Our `RadixSort` function requires space for at least two copies of each element: one place in the array and one place in the queue. If the queues are array-based, the amount of space is prohibitive because each queue must have room for every element. If the queues are linked, additional space for N pointers is required. We can cut the space requirements if we realize that this algorithm works just as well if the values to be sorted are in linked form. Nodes can be removed from the linked structure and moved to the appropriate queue; then the linked structure can be re-created by concatenating the queues. In this way, only one copy of an item (plus a pointer) exists, either in the linked structure or in a subgroup (queue).

Hence, both time and space requirements can be improved in the radix sort if we use the linked versions of the queue and list.

### 12.8 Parallel Merge Sort

Sorting, even with an O(N log[2]N) sort, can be very time consuming for a large data set. In the early days of computing, however, that was about the best that we could hope for because computers were designed to perform one operation at a time, called [serial](#bm01.xhtml_gloss126) or sequential processing. Modern computers, however, actually consist of multiple independent computer processors, called cores. Each core is typically designed to run two or more programs simultaneously, by duplicating some of the internal hardware components.

If we could take advantage of those capabilities for performing simultaneous operations within a sort, it could run even faster. Before the C++ 11 standard, there was no way to do so without using a third-party library of classes. But since then, support has been built into the language for what is known as [parallel processing](#bm01.xhtml_gloss098), and sorting provides an excellent opportunity to demonstrate it.

One of the conditions that is necessary in an algorithm for it to be a good candidate to take advantage of parallelism is that it must divide the work into independent pieces. When an algorithm has that quality, then it is easy to specify that the pieces can be computed at the same time. Thus, if a task has 50 independent pieces of work, and the computer can execute 50 independent programs (called threads) at once, we can theoretically gain a 50-fold improvement in performance.

We say “theoretically” because it takes some effort to create each thread, and that’s another form of overhead. Still, if there is a lot of work to do, the thread creation overhead will be comparatively small, and we can achieve a nearly maximal speed-up. If we’re sorting a large array of values, it can be well worth the effort to incorporate parallel processing.

Of the many sorting algorithms we’ve looked at, the one that is easiest to adapt is the Merge Sort. Recall that it begins by recursively dividing the array into pieces that are sorted independently and then merged. Those independent sorts are a prime example of potential parallelism.

Unlike our prior work analyses, in this section, we are interested in the best actual performance on a specific computer. Thus, we need to measure the processing time that the computer spends on the sort. How can we do this? You could have the program print a message before the sort and another afterward, and use a stopwatch to time the whole process. Unfortunately, unless you have incredibly quick reflexes, you’re unlikely to get accurate timing. Fortunately, most operating systems have built in timers, and C++ gives us access to them through a library called `chrono`. We simply write

```
#include <chrono>
```

At the start of our program, the library provides a template class called `time_point` and another type called `system_clock`, which can be used to define objects to hold high-precision time values:

```
chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> start;

chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> end;
```

The `system_clock` provides a function called `now` that returns the current time. So we can call it before the sort and assign the result to `start`, then call it after the sort and assign the result to `end`, as follows:

```
start = chrono::system_clock::now();

MergeSort<ItemType>(valuesArray, 0, MAX_ITEMS, tempArray);

end = chrono::system_clock::now();
```

The `chrono` library also provides a template class, called `duration`, that can hold the difference between two clock values as a time in seconds. We can then access that time using its `count` member function. For example:

```
chrono::duration<float> elapsed = end-start;

cout << "Execution time in seconds = " << elapsed.count() << "\n";
```

Here are all of the pieces, gathered together into a program that calls `MerrgeSort`, using `int` as the `ItemType`. The program begins by filling the array with random integers (using the `rand` function from `stdlib.h`), and then sorting it and reporting the execution time:

```
int main(int argc, const char * argv[])

{

  chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> start;

  chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> end;

  // Initialize the array with random integers

  for (int index = 0; index < MAX_ITEMS; index++)

  {

    numbers[index] = rand() % 1000000000;

  }

  start = chrono::system_clock::now();           // Record start time

  MergeSort<int>(numbers, 0, MAX_ITEMS-1, temp); // Run the sort

  end = chrono::system_clock::now();             // Record end time

  chrono::duration<float> elapsed = end-start;   // Report time

  cout << "Execution time in seconds = " << elapsed.count() << "\n";

  return 0;

}
```

When we run this with an array of 20 million values, it reports an execution time of approximately 8.2 seconds. We say “approximately” because the time varies by about 0.05 seconds from run to run. The reason is that the operating system is running other programs in the background, such as checking for email, and those compete randomly with our program for processing time.

In theory, on this machine, which is a quad-core processor, where each core can run two threads at once (with the potential of eight-way parallelism), we should be able to get the time down to just over a second. So let’s see how we can do that. We begin by importing another library:

```
#include <thread>
```

The `thread` class provides a constructor that takes a function as its first parameter. Following the function name, we list the arguments to the function. The constructor then tells the operating system to execute the function as a separate program, passing the arguments to it, and off it goes, doing whatever piece of work it needs to accomplish. Is it really that easy?

Almost! Once we turn the thread loose, we also have to check that it’s done before we try to use its results. That requires a second call to a function called `join`. When we call `join`, our program starts waiting. As soon as the thread sends a signal telling `join` that it has finished, our program continues on its way. We get parallelism by spawning multiple threads before calling `join` on any of them. We must call `join` on each thread before we use its results. Here’s how it looks for our `MergeSort` function:

```
template<class ItemType>

void MergeSort(ItemType values[], int first, int last, ItemType tempArray[])

// Post: The elements in values are sorted by key.

{

  if (first < last)

  {

    int middle = (first + last) / 2;

    thread left (MergeSort<ItemType>, values, first, middle, tempArray);

    thread right (MergeSort<ItemType>, values, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

    left.join();

    right.join();

    Merge<ItemType>(values, first, middle, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

  }

}
```

Each of the left and right sorts is spawned as a separate thread. Of course, each of those will recursively spawn a new pair of threads, so that we will eventually have as many threads as values. That should be more than enough to obtain all the potential parallelism on this machine. As before, we will run the sort on an array of `int` values. Let’s not be too ambitious to start, and just try an array of size 1,000.

Running the original `MergeSort` gives a time for this array of 0.000197 seconds. The parallel version reports 1.51943 seconds. That’s about 7,700 times slower! What happened? Remember what we said about overhead? When the sort reaches the lowest level of recursion, it is sorting a single value and returning it. That trivial amount of work is several thousand times less than the effort it takes to spawn a thread. So the overhead dominates the computation. In fact, for this particular machine, beyond about 1,000 threads, the program crashes because the operating system limits the number of threads that a single program can request. We clearly need a different strategy.

Each thread must have enough work to do to hide the overhead of creating it. Instead of generating a pair of threads at every level of recursion, we can switch after a few levels to just running the regular `MergeSort` function. How can we do that? One way is to pass another parameter that gets incremented at each level. Within the function we can check the level count and call the serial (nonparallel) version of the function. The trouble is that if the array is small, we can still end up generating threads with very little work.

What we want is a way to specify a quantity of work that is too small to bother with attempting to parallelize. We can add a parameter, `chunkSize`, to the parallel version of the sort. When `last-first` is greater than `chunkSize`, we recursively spawn threads to divide the work. Otherwise, we call the serial version of the sort to finish the small chunk of remaining work in this part of the call tree. Here, we show the code for the complete program, with the `Merge` function omitted (it’s unchanged):

```
#include <iostream>

#include <stdlib.h>

#include <thread>

#include <chrono>

using namespace std;

const int MAX_ITEMS = 20000000;

int numbers[MAX_ITEMS];

int temp[MAX_ITEMS];

int chunk;

// Merge function would appear here, but is omitted to save space

template<class ItemType>

void SerialMergeSort(ItemType values[], int first,

                     int last, ItemType tempArray[])

// Post: The elements in values are sorted by key.

{

  if (first < last)

  {

    int middle = (first + last) / 2;

    SerialMergeSort<ItemType>(values, first, middle, tempArray);

    SerialMergeSort<ItemType>(values, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

    Merge<ItemType>(values, first, middle, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

  }

}

template<class ItemType>

void ParallelMergeSort(ItemType values[], int first,

                       int last, ItemType tempArray[], int chunkSize)

// Post: The elements in values are sorted by key.

{

  if (first < last)

  {

    int middle = (first + last) / 2;

    if (last-first > chunkSize) // If enough work left, launch more threads

    {

      thread left (ParallelMergeSort<ItemType>, values, first,

                   middle, tempArray, chunkSize);

      thread right (ParallelMergeSort<ItemType>, values, middle + 1,

                   last, tempArray, chunkSize);

      left.join();

      right.join();

    }

    else                        // Otherwise finish sorting locally

    {

      SerialMergeSort<ItemType>(values, first, middle, tempArray);

      SerialMergeSort<ItemType>(values, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

    }

    Merge<ItemType>(values, first, middle, middle + 1, last, tempArray);

  }

}

int main(int argc, const char * argv[])

{

  chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> start;

  chrono::time_point<chrono::system_clock> end;

  // Initialize the array with random integers

  for (int index = 0; index < MAX_ITEMS; index++)

  {

    numbers[index] = rand() % 1000000000;

  }

  cout << "Enter chunk size (<= " << MAX_ITEMS << "): ";

  cin >> chunk;

  start = chrono::system_clock::now();           // Record start time

  ParallelMergeSort<int>(numbers, 0, MAX_ITEMS-1, temp, chunk); // Run sort

  end = chrono::system_clock::now();             // Record end time

  chrono::duration<float> elapsed = end-start;   // Report time

  cout << "Execution time in seconds = " << elapsed.count() << "\n";

  return 0;

}
```

Notice that instead of assigning a fixed chunk size, we let the user enter it. That will allow us to experiment with different sizes and see the effects. We have also set the array size back to 20 million in order to provide enough work to keep the processor busy. Notice, once again, that we are explicitly instantiating the template functions. In our original sort, the compiler could have inferred the types of the functions. But with the `thread` constructor, it cannot do that. You may have recognized that the `thread` constructor is unusual in being able to work with the arguments of another function, and the way that is accomplished in the library makes it impossible for the compiler to infer the template type. [Table 12.3](#ch12.xhtml_ch12table3) shows the results of a series of runs with different chunk sizes.

As you can see, once the number of threads reaches the potential parallelism of this particular computer, the time doesn’t diminish any further. When the chunk size falls below 25,000, the overhead starts to become a significant factor and the time increases. If the overhead is minimal for larger chunks, why didn’t the time decrease to one-eighth of the time for a single thread?

| Chunk Size | Number of Threads | Time (Seconds) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20,000,000 | 1 | 8.2 |
| 10,000,000 | 2 | 4.2 |
| 5,000,000 | 4 | 2.4 |
| 2,500,000 | 8 | 1.5 |
| 1,250,000 | 16 | 1.5 |
| 625,000 | 32 | 1.5 |
| 312,500 | 64 | 1.5 |
| 100,000 | 200 | 1.5 |
| 25,000 | 800 | 1.6 |

Table 12.3 Performance of Parallel Merge Sort

The answer is that we did not parallelize all the work. We launched threads for the sort functions, but after they join, the merge is still done serially. Could we parallelize that as well? The answer is yes, but it’s not as easy. The sorts divide the array into two sections, so each thread is working on its own half of the array. To make the merge parallel, we would need to split the arrays into two pairs that can be merged independently.

That means the values in the two pairs have to be in independent ranges. For example, suppose the two arrays to be merged contain values in the range 0\. . .999\. If we can divide them into two pairs of arrays, such that the first pair contains values in the range 0\. . .499 and the second pair contains 500\. . .999, then we can merge those pairs in parallel.

How can we split the arrays in this way? We must search the two arrays to find split point values that are in about the middle of their range. Since they are already in order, we can use a binary search to do that quickly. And we can split recursively to divide the arrays into more pieces that can be merged in parallel. But the splits depend on the data values and can thus result in pieces with significantly different sizes. For instance, in our preceding example, two-thirds of the values could be in the 0\. . .499 range.

Some of the pieces may be so small that there isn’t enough work to hide the overhead of thread creation. Conversely, a bad split could give the bulk of the work to one thread so that it takes almost as long as the serial merge. As you can see, parallelizing the merge step is complex and isn’t guaranteed to yield a significant improvement in performance.

There is one other aspect of parallel algorithms that we should mention. The merge combines values into a single array. By arranging the indexes carefully, all of those assignments will be to separate locations and won’t collide with each other. But consider what could happen if we tried to parallelize the radix sort by dividing the array among different threads that each write the values from their portion of the array to the various queues in parallel.

Each enqueue operation consists of multiple steps. In a linked representation, the key steps of enqueue are

```
if (rear == NULL)

  front = newNode;

else

  rear->next = newNode;

rear = newNode;
```

The problem is that threads can execute in any order. Thus, it is possible for one thread to change the `next` field of the `rear` element, and before it updates `rear`, another thread could come along and create its own `newNode` and set the `next` field to point to it instead. Thus, the first thread’s `newNode` is lost.

Avoiding such problems takes some careful coordination of when values are written, through an object called a `mutex`, which is an abbreviation of mutual exclusion. It is another class in the `thread` library that enables threads to obtain exclusive access to a data structure they are using. Handling concurrent accesses is a topic for a more advanced course on parallel algorithms. But we leave you with one last example to illustrate the kind of problems that can occur.

Here is a very simple threaded program:

```
#include <iostream>

#include <thread>

using namespace std;

void hello (int n){

  cout << "Hello, World #" << n << "\n";

}

int main(int argc, const char * argv[])

{

  thread first(hello, 1);

  thread second(hello, 2);

  cout << "Goodbye, World!\n";

  first.join();

  second.join();

  return 0;

}
```

It’s just a variation on that old standby, `HelloWorld`, that prints the message twice, each time in a separate thread, with an identifying number. Then it prints “Goodbye, World!” before exiting. What do you think will happen? We ran it three times, and got the following output:

```
Goodbye, World!

HHeelllloo,, WWoorrlldd ##2

1

Goodbye, World!

Hello, World #Hello, World #2

1

Goodbye, World!

Hello, World #1

Hello, World #2
```

As you can see, the output is randomly jumbled each time. The threads really are running simultaneously. The order in which they get the attention of the operating system to enqueue each character into the output buffer before it is displayed on the screen depends on what else the system is doing.

Parallel processing offers the potential for a significant improvement in performance. Our Parallel Merge Sort ran 5.5 times faster, on a machine for which a factor of 8 is the best we could achieve. When an algorithm offers such an easy path to exploiting multiple threads, it’s worth doing so. Many algorithms are not so simple to parallelize. In that case, we may be able to use more sophisticated techniques to get work done in parallel, or we might look for an alternate algorithm. Sometimes a slightly slower serial algorithm offers more opportunities for parallelism.

You might wonder whether using parallelism is really worth the effort. In our test cases, it shortened the sorting time from 8.2 to 1.5 seconds, which is hardly earth-shattering. But consider the difference that a factor of 5 would make in the time to predict tomorrow’s weather. If the forecast takes 50 hours instead of 10, it won’t come out until the day after tomorrow, which isn’t useful at all.

Also, the amount of parallelism available in computers is growing, such that 32- and 64-way parallelism are becoming commonplace. The graphics processors found in many computers already support thousands of parallel threads, although a special programming language is needed to use them. And super-computers, consisting of hundreds of thousands of processors, can run millions of threads. Knowing how to exploit parallelism is clearly a key skill in modern computer programming.

### Summary

We have not attempted in this chapter to describe every known sorting algorithm. Instead, we have presented a few of the most popular sorts, of which many variations exist. It should be clear from this discussion that no single sort works best for all applications. The simpler, generally O(N²) sorts work as well, and sometimes better, for fairly small values of N. Because they are simple, they require relatively little programmer time to write and maintain. As you add features to improve sorts, you also add to the complexity of the algorithms, increasing both the work required by the routines and the programmer time needed to maintain them.

Another consideration in choosing a sort algorithm is the order of the original data. If the data are already sorted (or almost sorted), `ShortBubble` is O(N), whereas some versions of a `QuickSort` are O(N²).

| Sort | Order of Magnitude |
| --- | --- |
| Best Case | Average Case | Worst Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SelectionSort` O(N²) | O(N²) | O(N²) |  |
| `BubbleSort` | O(N²) | O(N²) | O(N²) |
| `ShortBubble` | O(N) (*) | O(N²) | O(N²) |
| `InsertionSort` | O(N) (*) | O(N²) | O(N²) |
| `MergeSort` | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) |
| `QuickSort` | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) (depends on split) |
| `HeapSort` | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) | O(N log[2]N) |
|  
*Data almost sorted.

 |  |  |  |

Table 12.4 Comparison of Sorting Algorithms

As always, the first step in choosing an algorithm is to determine the goals of the particular application. This step usually narrows down the options considerably. After that, knowledge of the strong and weak points of the various algorithms assists you in making a choice. Even then, if performance is a critical goal, it may be necessary to run some experiments to find the variation of a sort that delivers optimal speed for a given computer system.

[Table 12.4](#ch12.xhtml_ch12table4) compares the sorts discussed in this chapter, in terms of Big-O. The radix sort is not shown in [Table 12.4](#ch12.xhtml_ch12table4) because it is not based on key comparisons. This sort algorithm uses the values in different key positions to successively divide the list into sublists and then collects the sublists back together. After this process is repeated as many times as there are positions in the key, the list is sorted.

To solve a problem, programmers often tend to think in terms of creating a new algorithm rather than adapting someone else’s solution. However, with a problem that has been as thoroughly explored as sorting, it is important to be familiar with the basic techniques. Sorts are higher-level tools that you will use repeatedly in many contexts. Just as carpenters must understand the capabilities and limitations of different kinds of saws, even though they all cut wood, you need to know which sorts are appropriate for different problems that involve ordering data.

Modern computers offer the potential for improving performance through the use of parallel processing. We saw how `MergeSort` is easily adapted to take advantage of parallelism because it begins by dividing up the work into independent pieces. Our simple implementation, using the C++ `thread` library, gave us 5.5-fold improvement in speed on a computer that could support eight-way parallelism. In the process, we encountered the issue of thread creation overhead and the need to give each thread enough work to hide that cost.

Our review of sorting techniques also gave us another opportunity to examine the capabilities and limitations of a measuring tool—the Big-O approximation—that helps us determine how much work is required by a particular algorithm. We saw another measuring tool, the system clock, that lets us measure actual processing time. Both building and measuring tools are needed to construct sound program solutions.
